Summary

NGS-DOSE measures the copy number of the 45S and 5S ribosomal DNA arrays, and of other sequence that reference genomes collapse, from aligned short-read genomes, which exist for hundreds of thousands of people. Standard analysis of those files does not report it, long-read assemblies leave the arrays in pieces, and read-depth ratios measure the library along with the person (section 1). Reads are assigned to a sequence class by class-specific 31-mers and counted as fragment ends; a per-library model of fragment-GC bias, fitted on 800 single-copy control regions, gives the expected count of any sequence, and the windows of the rDNA unit are calibrated across the cohort. No orthogonal assay of rDNA copy number exists for these samples, so the measurement is validated against sequence of known copy number in every genome, inheritance in trios, the same individuals sequenced on two technologies, and independent measurements of the same files.

In 620 genomes, held-out autosomal sequence reads 1.998 ± 0.008 copies (expected 2); chrX reads 0.990 ± 0.006 in men and 1.933 ± 0.025 in women with an intact culture (expected 1 and 2); chrY reads 0.975 ± 0.014 in men and at most 0.007 in women (expected 1 and 0). Sex inferred from the reads agrees with the pedigree in 620 of 620. The distal junction, present once on each acrocentric short arm, reads 9.658 ± 0.334 (expected 10); departures from the cohort's level are whole copies (37 carriers), transmitted in 7 of 20 carrier-parent–child pairs and de novo in 0. The targeted fetch returns 0.9997 of the whole-file scan's 45S estimate (620 genomes; range 0.9992–0.9999). Run on the fetch counts alone, the cohort layer and the trio test give the same answer: 45S reliability 1.00 (0.93–1.30) against 1.00 from the scans.

In 114 trios the calibrated 45S estimate has a transmission reliability of 1.00 (0.93–1.30); traits that are not transmitted read near zero (held-out autosomal sequence -0.17, mitochondrial content 0.09). In 12 individuals sequenced on two technologies, the test–retest intraclass correlation is 0.98 for the calibrated estimate and 0.19 for the 18S depth ratio (0.87 after removing its offset between technologies). Within one chemistry the depth ratio follows each library's GC bias (r = 0.86); under the fragment-GC model it does not (r = 0.15). Against the published estimates of Hall et al. (2021) for the same files, r = 0.984 on 473 shared samples; their exclusion of duplicate-flagged reads accounts for the offset. NGS-PCA's coverage-based mitochondrial copy number for the same files agrees with ours at r = 0.996 (theirs 0.92× ours, the duplicate flag again), its chrX ratio at r = 0.9998. 7 of 10 satellite families track HPRC assemblies of 6 of these individuals with r ≥ 0.95.

What is not shown: the absolute scale of the rDNA rests on unit windows on which three Illumina chemistries agree, not on an assay; 5S transmission is undecided at this number of trios; every sample is a lymphoblastoid cell line sequenced with one chemistry and one pipeline.

1. Rationale

Each human genome carries several hundred copies of the 45S ribosomal DNA unit, about 45 kb long, in tandem arrays on the short arms of the five acrocentric chromosomes, and a tandem array of the 5S unit on chromosome 1. A single array spans from 50 kb to more than 6 Mb, the two homologues of a chromosome almost never carry arrays of one size, and an array is rearranged in more than one meiosis in ten (Stults et al., Genome Res 2008). Total copy number varies severalfold between individuals and is heritable.

Why a method is needed

Short-read genomes are the only genomes that exist at population scale: 490,640 in UK Biobank alone (UK Biobank Whole-Genome Sequencing Consortium, Nature 2025), where rDNA copy number estimated from them has been associated with blood-cell counts and kidney function (Rodriguez-Algarra, Evans & Rakyan, Cell Genomics 2024) and with metabolic disease (Raj et al., medRxiv 2026, a preprint). At that size a correlation of 0.01 between an estimate and a trait has p ≈ 2 × 10−12, so whatever an estimate carries of the library, rather than the person, becomes a finding wherever the library also tracks the trait. Standard analysis does not give the number, and read-depth ratios, long reads and laboratory assays each fall short on scale or on the library (below). What is needed is a measurement that finds every rDNA read wherever the aligner put it (3.3), predicts each library's count of GC-rich sequence from single-copy sequence in the same genome (3.5), holds its scale across chemistries (3.4), does not depend on the duplicate flag (3.7), reads a small part of each file (3.3), and shows in every genome that it reads known copy numbers correctly (3.1, 3.2). NGS-DOSE is one way to meet these. The tests on this page apply to any other, including the estimators of the studies above, and the 18S depth ratio is carried beside it throughout so that the difference can be seen.

Standard analysis
Reports no copy number. GRCh38 carries fewer than ten copies of the 45S transcribed region, on chr21 and two small contigs, where a genome has hundreds; the reads of every unit fall on those copies with no unique alignment, and variant and copy-number callers mask the loci.
Read-depth ratio
Depth on the reference's rDNA relative to depth elsewhere in the genome, as in published studies (Gibbons et al., Nat Commun 2014; Hall et al., Sci Rep 2021; Rodriguez-Algarra et al. 2024), runs on existing files. Without a model of the library it measures the library along with the person: the rDNA is GC-rich, parts of the unit drop out by amounts that depend on the chemistry, and the duplicate flag marks 5.1% of 45S reads against 8.8% of single-copy reads, so dropping flagged reads moves the ratio by a different amount in every genome (the two rates' ratio runs from 0.43 to 0.82). In UK Biobank its mean differs between the two sequencing centres (Rodriguez-Algarra et al. 2024). Here, within one chemistry the 18S ratio's departure from the calibrated estimate follows each library's GC bias (r = 0.86; 3.5); the same people read 27% lower by it on the older of two technologies (intraclass correlation 0.19, against 0.98 for the calibrated estimate; 3.4).
Long reads
The units are near-identical, which defeats assembly. Even in T2T-CHM13, three of the five arrays are model sequences, because ultra-long nanopore reads were not long enough to order their units (Nurk et al., Science 2022); in 156 acrocentric short arms assembled from HiFi, ultra-long nanopore and Hi-C data, the rDNA array collapsed in every one (Lin et al., Cell 2026). Long reads, imaging and methylation have given the size and activity of each array in fifteen genomes (Potapova et al., Cell Genomics 2025). Of the genomes counted here, 6 have an HPRC release-2 assembly; these hold 35% (28–41%) of the rDNA the measured copy number implies, in stretches no longer than 1.05 Mb, where the average array would be 2.5 Mb (data/rdna_hprc.tsv).
Molecular assays
Droplet digital PCR is precise (CHM13: 409 ± 9 copies; Nurk et al. 2022) and pulsed-field gels size single arrays (Stults et al. 2008), but each needs the DNA and a laboratory assay per person: in a biobank, every participant's stored DNA.

The case is strongest for the rDNA. Long-read assemblies close most satellite arrays and are their truth here (3.8), so for the satellites it is one of scale alone; telomeric content already has short-read estimators (Ding et al., Nucleic Acids Res 2014), and the class measured here is a relative one.

How the measurement is judged

Whether the measurement is correct cannot be settled by comparison with an assay, because none exists for these samples. It can be settled by comparison with what is known: (i) sequence of known copy number in every sample, measured by the same code; (ii) Mendelian transmission in the cohort's 603 trios; (iii) the same individuals sequenced on different technologies; (iv) an independent estimate from the same files; (v) long-read assemblies, for the satellite arrays measured by the same k-mer method. Each comparison excludes a different failure. The results are presented in that order.

2. Methods

Samples
The expanded 1000 Genomes cohort: 3,202 individuals in 26 populations, including 603 trios, sequenced by the New York Genome Center to about 30× (Illumina NovaSeq, 2×150 bp, PCR-free) and aligned to GRCh38 with decoy and HLA contigs (Byrska-Bishop et al., Cell 2022). All DNA is from lymphoblastoid cell lines. Counting runs on the public CRAMs; 620 genomes have been counted so far, 620 in both modes, with 114 of 603 trios complete.
Class assignment
Every 31-mer of every read is tested against a panel of class-diagnostic k-mers: k-mers of the class's unit sequence (45S, KY962518.1; 5S, X12811.1; distal junction, 400 kb of CHM13 chr21) that occur nowhere in GRCh38 or T2T-CHM13 outside the class's own loci. A read with at least four panel k-mers is assigned to the class and placed on the unit by its hits; its alignment position is not used. Experimental panels built from the CHM13 CenSat annotation add ten satellite families and the telomeric repeat.
Counting
Fragment 5′ ends are counted: per 50-bp bin and strand of the unit for class reads, and per position in 800 single-copy control regions (10.1 Mb) for the library model. Scan mode reads the whole CRAM; fetch mode retrieves only the control regions and 80 sink intervals (3.3 Mb) where the NYGC pipeline places class reads, learned from whole-file scans of two genomes.
Library model
A Poisson spline of fragment-end density on fragment GC content is fitted per sample on the control regions. The expected count of any sequence follows from its fragment-GC composition; the copy number of each 250-bp window of a unit is 2 × observed / expected.
Calibration
Windows of the 45S unit drop out beyond what the GC curve predicts, by amounts that depend on the sequencing chemistry. Per-window efficiencies are learned across the cohort by median polish; the absolute scale is set by anchor windows on which three Illumina chemistries agreed in the pilot. Two comparators are carried alongside: a single-sample estimate from the anchor windows alone, and the 18S read-depth ratio used in the literature, with no GC model and no calibration.
Known-truth controls
80 held-out autosomal regions (two copies), 60 chrX regions (one in men, two in women) and 40 X-degenerate chrY regions (one, none), measured by the alignment-position path; and the distal junction, present once on each of the ten acrocentric short arms, measured by the k-mer path with its class restricted to k-mers that occur exactly once in each of the five CHM13 junctions. Mitochondrial genomes and EBV episomes per cell are measured as covariates of the culture.
Transmission
For each estimator, the regression of child on midparent in complete trios. Reliability R = b − ρ(1 − b), with b the midparent slope and ρ the spousal correlation after centring within population; 95% intervals by family bootstrap at 20 trios or more; paired bootstrap for differences between estimators. Held-out autosomal sequence (no true variance) and mitochondrial and EBV content (not in the nuclear genome) are the negative controls.
Technical structure
Principal components of the control regions' residual depth after the GC model. The number retained is chosen at the Marchenko–Pastur edge of the noise bulk and checked by a cross-validated sweep against the known truths and the trios. NGS-PCA's genome-wide coverage PCs are applied where available.
External comparisons
The pilot's twelve genomes have an independent older library of the same cell line (HGSVC, HiSeq 2500 2×126, 2015; Illumina Platinum, HiSeq 2000 2×100, 2012–13), compared with anchor windows chosen with the family held out. Hall, Turner & Queitsch (Sci Rep 2021) published 18S copy number for 2,419 of these CRAMs as read depth relative to chromosome 1 with duplicate-flagged reads excluded. HPRC release-2 assemblies of cohort samples give the size of every satellite array (CenSat annotation, both haplotypes); a class is compared only where arrays containing gaps are immaterial. NGS-PCA's per-sample QC for the same cohort (mosdepth, 1-kb bins, duplicate-flagged reads excluded) gives mitochondrial copies per cell, the X and Y coverage ratios and the autosomal depth by a coverage route.
Provenance
Engine builds: 0.1.0+fae1124 (620). Resource bundle GRCh38-v1; panel 9ab0a0e8,a23ef9ed,7f3b4c3c, controls 184ab16e, sinks 9dd52ba1 (SHA-256 prefixes; one of each means one cohort). Read length 150; placement grid 1000 bp. Every input carried its end-of-file marker.

61 sample(s) carry a flag (aneuploid chromosome, sex mismatch, mosaic loss of an X or Y, a distal-junction step, low depth, another engine build); they are marked in the sample table and listed in data/flags.tsv. A flag marks something to examine, not a verdict.

3.1 Sequence of known copy number, in every genome

If the model is right, held-out autosomal sequence reads 2, chrX reads 1 in men and 2 in women, chrY reads 1 and 0, and the distal junction reads 10, in every genome. Held-out autosomal sequence reads 1.998 ± 0.008 copies (n = 620). chrX reads 0.990 ± 0.006 in 292 men and 1.933 ± 0.025 in the 313 women whose culture has kept both X chromosomes (at least 1.85 copies); 15 women read below that. chrY reads 0.975 ± 0.014 in men with an intact Y and 0.0026 in women (maximum 0.0066); 6 men read below 0.85. The distal junction reads 9.658 ± 0.334 (cohort-calibrated). Women read the X and every genome reads the distal junction a few percent below expectation; both are late-replicating sequence, which DNA from a growing culture under-represents (section 4).

Sex inferred from the reads (a Y above 0.1 copies) agrees with the pedigree in 620 of 620 samples.

A woman whose X reads well below 2, or a man whose Y does, has lost that chromosome in part of the cell culture: the known behaviour of lymphoblastoid lines, and a reason the controls are measured in every sample.

3.2 The distal junction changes in whole copies, and the changes are inherited

Ten distal junctions is the norm; a rearranged acrocentric short arm leaves nine, and a Robertsonian translocation, which fuses two acrocentrics and loses both short arms, leaves eight. Copy number relative to the cohort's level (9.65) should therefore sit near a whole number, and a step, being a structural variant, should be transmitted to half of a carrier's children and arise de novo in almost none. Within ±0.3 of a step: 4 genomes at −2, 16 at −1, 526 at 0, 17 at +1; the main mode has a robust SD of 0.13 copies and 37 genomes sit between steps.

Where a carrier parent and a child were both counted, the step was transmitted in 7 of 20 (the expectation for a heterozygous variant is one half); no child carries a step that neither parent has. The distal junction is measured by the same k-mer path as the rDNA. A change of one copy in ten, seen in a parent and again in the child, shows that the path resolves multi-copy acrocentric sequence to a single copy.

3.4 The same individuals on two sequencing technologies

The pilot's 12 genomes were also sequenced years earlier on a different instrument, with different read length, insert size, depth, alignment pipeline and a GC response the reverse of NovaSeq's. Agreement between the two libraries of a person, per estimator (the calibrated estimate with anchor windows chosen with the person's family held out, so the cross-technology level is out of sample):

The 5S unit is 68% GC throughout and has no anchor windows, so its estimate rests on the GC model alone and carries an offset of 17% between technologies at a pair SD of 0.040. The distal junction does not vary between people, so its intraclass correlation is near zero by construction; its within-person CV of 1.8% is the figure that matters.

The intraclass correlation measures absolute agreement, so an offset between technologies counts against it: the depth ratio's -27% offset is a property of the library, not of the person, and removing it as a batch effect leaves an ICC of 0.87 against 0.98 for the calibrated estimate, whose offset is 2%. The two DNA batches were drawn from different cultures of each line, so these figures bound measurement error from above. This is the comparison that distinguishes the calibrated estimate from a depth ratio; within one chemistry (3.6) it cannot be seen.

3.5 What the fragment-GC model removes

Libraries differ in GC bias even within one chemistry: the rate at which 65%-GC fragments were sequenced, relative to each library's mean, runs from 1.17 to 1.29 across the middle 80% of genomes, and the rDNA is GC-rich. The 18S depth ratio divided by the calibrated estimate of the same genome follows that bias with r = 0.86 (0.84 to 0.88) (n = 620); the same 18S region under the fragment-GC model, r = 0.15 (0.07 to 0.22). Within the cohort the effect is a few percent (SD of the log ratio 0.034), small next to the 22% by which people differ, which is why it does not show in the trios; between technologies (3.4) it is 27%.

3.6 Transmission in trios

A child's dosage is the mean of the parents' plus segregation; measurement error is not inherited. The midparent slope therefore measures the share of an estimate's variance that is real, its reliability, for each estimator separately. Two traits of the same genomes that are not transmitted run beside them as negative controls: held-out autosomal sequence, which has error but no true variance, and the mitochondrial and EBV content of the culture, which vary but are not in the nuclear genome.

114 complete trios.

Every metric the cohort measures was put to the same test, in four groups: the rDNA estimators, whose transmission is the claim; the satellite arrays, whose mass is a property of the genome and must be inherited (positive controls); sequence of known copy number, which has nothing to inherit except the distal junction's whole-copy steps (3.2); and the culture's and the library's properties, which are not in the nuclear genome (negative controls). A method that measured library artefacts would light up the last group; one that measured nothing would light up none. HSat1B lives mostly on Yq and passes from father to son only, so its midparent statistics are diluted by design. The last column repeats the reliability with the cohort layer and the trio test run on the fetch counts alone (3.3).

Reliability is capped at 1; a slope above 1 is noise around 1, and the interval says how much. A spousal correlation far from zero means members of a family share something other than DNA (a batch), and every reliability in the table is inflated by about as much. The negative-control rows should read near zero.

The 45S reliability is 1.00 (0.93 to 1.30); the interval allows a measurement error of at most 6.2% of a person's value. The variation measured is therefore inherited. Because people differ in 45S copy number by a CV of 22% and every estimator errs by a few percent, every estimator has a reliability near 1 within one cohort and one pipeline, and the trios cannot rank them: the paired differences below are the test, and they are small. Ranking rests on the comparison across technologies (3.4).

The 5S array reads 0.70 (0.25 to 1.08) at 114 trios: an interval too wide to say whether its copy number is transmitted like the 45S's. Its spread between people is as large, its estimate as precise, and it reproduced across technologies in the pilot (3.4); the full cohort decides.

3.7 An independent pipeline on the same files

On the 473 genomes shared so far with Hall, Turner & Queitsch (2021), their 18S value against our 18S depth ratio with no GC model, halved to their per-haploid scale: r = 0.984, their values 1.072× ours. Re-applying their exclusion of duplicate-flagged reads to our counts brings the ratio to 1.028 (SD 0.036): the offset is the duplicate flag, which marks fewer reads inside the collapsed rDNA than outside it (section 4). Against the calibrated estimate (rDNA45S.cn/2): r = 0.959, ratio 1.219.

NGS-PCA's coverage QC on the same files

NGS-PCA computes, from mosdepth coverage of the same CRAMs in 1-kb bins with duplicate-flagged reads excluded, mitochondrial copies per cell as twice the chrM mean coverage over the median autosomal coverage, and the X and Y coverage ratios. On the 620 shared genomes, mitochondrial copies per cell agree at r = 0.996 (0.995 to 0.996), theirs 0.921× ours (10–90% 0.898–0.938; SD of the log ratio 0.018); chrX at r = 0.9998, ratio 1.003; autosomal depth at r = 0.984, theirs 0.88× ours. Sex inferred by the two agrees in 620 of 620. The 15 women and 6 men whose cultures have lost part of an X or a Y read the same by both routes (for example HG00154: 1.32 here, 1.33 there). The chrY ratio in men is compressed and noisier by the coverage route (median 0.80 in men with an intact Y, r = 0.47 against our 40 X-degenerate regions), since a whole-chromosome mean includes sequence that maps poorly. The mitochondrial offset lies in the direction of the duplicate flag, which mosdepth honours and NGS-DOSE does not: a 16.6-kb genome at several thousand-fold depth saturates the positions a duplicate marker can distinguish, and the ratio falls with depth (r = -0.41).

3.8 Satellite arrays against long-read assemblies

Assemblies collapse the rDNA and are no truth for it (section 1), but 6 of these genomes have HPRC release-2 assemblies whose CenSat annotation gives the size of every satellite array: the same kind of sequence, measured by the same k-mer machinery. A genome is compared in a class only when the arrays its assembly did not close are immaterial. HSat1A, HSat1B, HSat3, bSat, aSatHOR, ACRO, CER track the assemblies across people with r ≥ 0.95.

3.9 Technical structure: coverage PCs

The residual depth of the 800 control regions after the GC model carries whatever library and sample structure is left; its principal components are technical covariates computed on sequence disjoint from every class. Marchenko-Pastur edge: 13 components clear the noise bulk (n = 620 x p = 800; edge 1.566 fitted on the leading 93 of 620 singular values; noise SD ~0.0295; edge 1.09x as broad as equal-variance noise would make it).

Regressing out the 13 components above the edge removes this share of each estimate's variance (log scale), against what 13 random regressors would remove by chance:

columnvariance removedexpected by chanceadjusted R²
rDNA45S.cn4.804%2.100%2.762%
rDNA45S.cn_single4.853%2.100%2.812%
rDNA45S.18S.flat5.559%2.100%3.533%
rDNA5S.cn1.306%2.100%-0.811%
DJ.cn8.497%2.100%6.534%
truth.auto34.537%2.100%33.133%
chrM.copies13.953%2.100%12.107%
chrEBV.copies17.726%2.100%15.961%

The components find technical variance where it exists: 35% of the held-out autosomal estimate's variance, which is nothing but error, against 5% of the 45S estimate's (2.1% expected by chance). With a measurement error of a few percent and a between-person CV of 22%, the technical share of the 45S variance is small; the GC model and the calibration do the work, and the PCs are insurance.

The sweep, 0 to 26 control PCs regressed out, cross-validated: the known truths say when adjustment stops removing noise; transmission (114 trios) says when it starts removing signal. One-standard-error picks: truth.auto: 1, truth.chrX: 7, truth.chrY: 0, DJ.cn: 9, rDNA45S.cn: 0, rDNA45S.cn_single: 0, rDNA45S.18S.flat: 0, rDNA5S.cn: 0.

NGS-PCA coverage PCs: Marchenko-Pastur edge: 40 components clear the noise bulk (n = 3,200 x p = 142,070; edge 54.72 fitted on the leading 200 of 200 singular values; noise SD ~0.126; edge 1.56x as broad as equal-variance noise would make it); 618 of the genomes have them.

The 45S array holds 454 copies per diploid genome in the median person (10–90%: 342–583; range 183–847; n = 620), the 5S array 175 (129–234).

The cell line

Every genome was sequenced from a lymphoblastoid cell line, whose state leaves marks on coverage. Mitochondrial genomes per cell: median 749 (10–90%: 620–945); EBV episomes per cell: median 39.0 (16.1–94.6). Both vary far more between people than the rDNA does and neither is inherited through the nuclear genome, which is why they serve as negative controls in 3.6.

Satellite arrays and the telomeric repeat

Satellite arrays are dispersed over the alignment, so only a whole-file scan measures them. Diploid mass per family; what each panel can see was measured on the genome it was built from (four families are relative measures, under-read by their k-mer recall).

5. Limitations

  • No absolute calibration. No orthogonal assay of rDNA copy number exists for these samples. The absolute level rests on unit windows on which three Illumina chemistries agree; the known truths test the model and the k-mer path, not the absolute scale of the rDNA.
  • Cell-line DNA. Every sample is a lymphoblastoid line; its replication state, EBV load and mitochondrial content are measured but not removed. Blood-derived genomes will not carry the first of these.
  • Trios bound reliability from above where members of a family were prepared together; the spousal correlation is the check. Because the rDNA varies far more between people than any estimator errs, trios show that the measured variation is real, not which estimator measures it best.
  • One chemistry, one pipeline. The cohort is NovaSeq 2×150 aligned by one pipeline; the cross-technology evidence is twelve genomes. DRAGEN alignments and other chemistries are untested.
  • The satellite panels were built from one genome (CHM13). Four of the ten families are relative measures; HSat2 is unjudged until assemblies without gaps in it have been compared. The telomere class is a relative measure of (TTAGGG)n content, not a telomere length.
  • Partial cohort. 620 of 3,202: population comparisons and the number of complete trios depend on which genomes have landed.

6. Data and reproducibility

The counts files under counts_scan/ and counts_fetch/ are the primary data: about 240 kB per whole-file scan and 70 kB per fetch, no reads, no genotypes. Everything above is computed from them:

pip install ngsdose        # or: apptainer pull ngs-dose.sif docker://ghcr.io/jlanej/ngs-dose:latest
ngsdose report --scan counts_scan/ --fetch counts_fetch/ -p pedigree.txt --hall hall2021_MOESM1.txt --pilot pilot/ --qc ngspca_sample_qc.tsv -o docs/

Tables behind every figure: data/cohort.tsv (one row per genome, every column), data/modes.tsv, data/transmission.tsv and data/trios.tsv (every trio's values), data/fetch_check.tsv, data/pcsweep.tsv, data/satellites_hprc.tsv, data/rdna_hprc.tsv, data/flags.tsv; the numbers in the prose, report.json; the trio assessment as a document, trio_report.pdf. The counts were made by ngs-dose count (0.1.0+fae1124 (620)) from the 1000 Genomes 30× CRAMs (Byrska-Bishop et al., Cell 2022; AWS Open Data) with the GRCh38-v1 resource bundle. Method, design document and audit: github.com/jlanej/NGS-DOSE.
